Remarks – Y-200 display flickering trend (June 2023)

Over the last four weeks we have seen DISP-FLICK appear on the Y-200 line at a noticeably higher rate than on the Z-300 or DR-6. In May the Y-200 averaged 1.25 flicker defects per batch of 400 inspected units. In June that average has risen to 3.5 per batch. The defect presents as an intermittent flicker on the display panel, typically appearing 10–15 minutes after power-on and lasting for short intervals. It does not appear to affect touch response or brightness stability when the flicker is not active.

Model Y-200 most_common_defect display flickering. Record status: current.

The Z-300 also shows DISP-FLICK but at a much lower rate – roughly 1 per 500 units inspected. The DR-6 has not recorded a single display flicker defect in the same period, which rules out a plant-wide environmental cause such as line voltage fluctuation or ESD issues, since all three models run through the same final assembly area.

On 2023-06-21 we noted that the Y-200 display panel supplier changed from OptiView Displays to BrightLink Components for the panels used in batches B23-117 onward. The first batch with the new panels (B23-117) had 3 flicker defects, and the subsequent two Y-200 batches (B23-121 and B23-125) had 4 and 5 respectively. This is a clear upward step compared to the previous supplier's panels. However, we cannot yet confirm a causal link – the sample size is small, and we have not received the incoming inspection results for the BrightLink panels beyond the standard visual and electrical checks.

The seal lot 2306-18 was received at the Melbourne warehouse on 19 June and distributed to both Melbourne and Sydney lines. The housing supplier, Apex Castings, changed their die-cast release agent formulation in early June, and we have seen a slight increase in surface porosity rejects in incoming inspection for housings received after 12 June. That would fit the fact that most of the leaks in B23-132 were found on the final functional test bench, not during the static pressure check.

**2023-02-20 – Motor Overheating Investigation Update (Inspector PK, Sydney)**

Following the 3rd-party audit of the motor supplier requested in B23-007, preliminary findings were received today. The audit covered production runs from October 2022 through January 2023. This aligns with the elevated MOTOR-OVH counts observed in WM-7 batches since late December. The supplier has agreed to implement corrective action, including 100% inspection of stator windings for the next four weeks. We will monitor B23-037 onward to assess whether defect rates return to expected levels. Historical data for Model X-100 shows a defect rate of 12.5 defects per thousand units across 2022–2023; the current WM-7 batches are running above that historical baseline, confirming the need for the corrective action. Quality Inspection Log – Melbourne & Sydney (2023–2024)

Remarks – Y-200 display flickering trend (June 2023)

Over the last four weeks we have seen DISP-FLICK appear on the Y-200 line at a noticeably higher rate than on the Z-300 or DR-6. In May the Y-200 averaged 1.25 flicker defects per batch of 400 inspected units. In June that average has risen to 3.5 per batch. The defect presents as an intermittent flicker on the display panel, typically appearing 10–15 minutes after power-on and lasting for short intervals. It does not appear to affect touch response or brightness stability when the flicker is not active.

Model Y-200 most_common_defect display flickering. Record status: current.

The Z-300 also shows DISP-FLICK but at a much lower rate – roughly 1 per 500 units inspected. The DR-6 has not recorded a single display flicker defect in the same period, which rules out a plant-wide environmental cause such as line voltage fluctuation or ESD issues, since all three models run through the same final assembly area.

On 2023-06-21 we noted that the Y-200 display panel supplier changed from OptiView Displays to BrightLink Components for the panels used in batches B23-117 onward. The first batch with the new panels (B23-117) had 3 flicker defects, and the subsequent two Y-200 batches (B23-121 and B23-125) had 4 and 5 respectively. This is a clear upward step compared to the previous supplier's panels. However, we cannot yet confirm a causal link – the sample size is small, and we have not received the incoming inspection results for the BrightLink panels beyond the standard visual and electrical checks.

We have requested from the supplier the test data for the display driver IC and the LVDS cable assembly used in the Y-200. The flicker could be a panel issue, but it could equally be an intermittent connection in the cable harness that seats differently with the new panel's connector layout. The Melbourne line has been using the same harness part number since January, so a change in the panel's connector pinout or mechanical tolerance could cause a poor contact that only shows up under vibration or thermal cycling.

Action items:
- PK to pull the last 10 Y-200 batches from the MES and check the serial number ranges against the panel lot numbers.
- JL to coordinate with incoming inspection on the BrightLink panel batch certificates – specifically the contrast ratio and response time measurements.
- QA to hold the current BrightLink panel lot (BL-2306-14) pending further investigation, and to advise production planning that we may need to revert to OptiView stock if the trend continues.

**Note on B23-132 (2023-07-04, SYD):**

Ten leaking seals in one batch is well above the running average for the Z-300 (about 1.4% over the last 40 batches). I pulled the seal lot traceability from the MES: units in B23-132 used seal lot 2306-18, the same lot used in B23-130 (MEL) which also showed a higher-than-normal leak count. The previous two Z-300 batches, B23-126 and B23-128, used lot 2306-11 and had 2 and 3 leaks respectively.

The seal itself is a nitrile O-ring, part number SR-447, supplied by FlexiSeal Industries. We have not changed the part number or the supplier. The seal lot 2306-18 was received at the Melbourne warehouse on 19 June and distributed to both Melbourne and Sydney lines. Incoming inspection at the time passed the lot on hardness (Shore A 72–75) and dimensional checks (ID 24.9–25.1 mm, cross-section 2.9–3.1 mm). There is no record of any storage temperature excursions in the warehouse log for that period.

Model Z-300 most_common_defect leaking seal. Record status: current.

What changed around the same time? The Melbourne line switched to a new seal installation tool on 22 June (tool changeover record TC-2023-06-22). Sydney has been using the older pneumatic press. If the tool is the cause, we would expect Melbourne to be worse than Sydney. But B23-132 (Sydney) had 10 leaks and B23-130 (Melbourne) had 8, so the tool change does not explain the Sydney count.

Another possibility is the pump housing casting. The housing supplier, Apex Castings, changed their die-cast release agent formulation in early June, and we have seen a slight increase in surface porosity rejects in incoming inspection for housings received after 12 June. A porous surface under the seal could cause a slow weep that only shows up after the unit has been running for a few hours. That would fit the fact that most of the leaks in B23-132 were found on the final functional test bench, not during the static pressure check.

I have asked the lab to do a cross-section on three of the leaking seals from B23-132 to check for compression set or nicks. Results due by Friday. In the meantime, I am holding the remaining stock of seal lot 2306-18 (about 4,200 pieces) in quarantine until we have a better picture.
